description: Compute rise, set, and culmination (transit) times for a body at an observer location, plus the maximum altitude at culmination. For the Sun, also returns the three twilight pairs (civil −6°, nautical −12°, astronomical −18°) so a single call answers "when does the sun set and when is it truly dark." Each pair covers the night after the cycle's set (after its culmination when it has none) — dusk that evening, dawn the next morning — so the dawn listed beside a sunrise is the following day's. A depth a night never reaches (astronomical twilight around midsummer at mid-to-high latitudes) is null for that night. When `start` falls between sunset and sunrise, the first cycle opens at the next sunrise and `night_in_progress` carries the night already under way, dusk through dawn, including times before `start` that have passed; otherwise, for the dawn before a sunrise, read the previous cycle or start a day earlier. Searches forward from `start` (default today) and returns the next `count` cycles (default 1), up to 31 per call: a larger `count`, up to 366, returns the first 31 and a notice naming the exact `start` and `count` that continue the series, or saying no call can when the next cycle starts after 2100; a continuation started just past a sunset repeats in `night_in_progress` the night the last cycle of the previous call carried, while its cycles pick up without overlap. When the body is already above the horizon at `start`, the first cycle is the interval in progress: its `set` is the imminent one and its `rise` is null, since that rise precedes the search — so a set is never reported earlier than the rise beside it. Circumpolar or never-rises situations are reported as null rise/set fields with an explanatory note rather than an error — the fact is the answer. One cycle covers one day: a day the body neither rises nor sets on (polar night, midnight sun) is a cycle of its own, so consecutive cycles are consecutive days and each night appears in exactly one cycle. When `start` falls after the culmination of such a polar-night day, or after the last sunset before one, the first cycle is the rest of that day — rise, set, and transit null — carrying the twilight of that night, including times before `start` that have passed. Default elevation is 0 m; pass an IANA `timezone` for observer-local times. This server does not geocode — resolve coordinates upstream first.

body.description: The body to compute rise/set for. Twilight is included only when this is "sun".

count.description: Number of forward rise/set cycles to return. Default 1. At most 31 are computed per call; a count up to 366 returns the first 31 with a notice naming the `start` and `count` that continue the series.

elevation.description: Observer elevation in meters above sea level. Default 0.

latitude.description: Observer latitude in decimal degrees, north positive.

longitude.description: Observer longitude in decimal degrees, east positive.

start.description: Search start as an ISO 8601 UTC string, e.g. "2024-06-21T00:00:00Z". Defaults to now. A value with no zone designator is read as UTC, not the local zone of the server process.

timezone.description: IANA timezone for localized output, e.g. "America/Los_Angeles". When omitted, output is UTC-only.

name: astronomy_get_rise_set

body.description: The body these rise/set cycles are for, echoed from the request.

cap.description: The per-call cycle cap that was applied.

error.description: Present when the call failed. Absent on success.

code.description: JSON-RPC error code for this failure.

reason.description: Machine-readable failure mode. Declared by this tool: `invalid_time`: The `start` value is not a parseable ISO 8601 instant, or names a calendar date that does not exist (e.g. 2026-02-30). `time_out_of_range`: The requested start instant is outside the engine's high-accuracy span (≈1900–2100). `invalid_timezone`: The `timezone` value is not an IANA zone this runtime knows. Other values are possible when a failure originates below the handler.

recovery.description: Actionable next step for the caller.

message.description: Human-readable description of what went wrong.

events.description: One entry per rise/set/transit cycle, searching forward from the start time.

items.description: One rise/set/transit cycle, with twilight when the body is the Sun.

note.description: Explanatory note when a rise or set is absent (e.g. "Circumpolar — never sets at this latitude/date.").

rise_local.description: Rise time in observer-local time, present only when a timezone was supplied.

rise_utc.description: Rise time in ISO 8601 UTC, or null when the body does not rise in this cycle — because it is circumpolar, or because it was already above the horizon when the cycle opened (at the search start, or after a day it never set on), so its rise precedes the cycle. The accompanying note says which.

set_local.description: Set time in observer-local time, present only when a timezone was supplied.

set_utc.description: Set time in ISO 8601 UTC, or null when the body does not set in this cycle.

transit_altitude_degrees.description: Maximum altitude in degrees at culmination, or null when not found.

transit_local.description: Culmination time in observer-local time, present only when a timezone was supplied.

transit_utc.description: Culmination (highest point) time in ISO 8601 UTC, or null when it falls outside this cycle — before its rise, after its set, or before the search start.

twilight.description: The three twilight pairs, present only when body is "sun". Each pair spans one night: dusk is the evening of this cycle's set — or, in a cycle with no set, the evening after its culmination — and dawn is the following morning, so a cycle's dawn falls a day after its rise. Each is searched only up to the start of the next cycle's day (its sunrise, or its culmination when it has no rise), so a depth the night never reaches is null. A first cycle with no rise, set, or transit is the rest of the day the search started in, inside or at the edge of a polar night; its pairs can include times before `start` that have passed. The dawn before a given sunrise is in the previous cycle's pair; before the first cycle's sunrise it is in `night_in_progress` when `start` falls in a night that began with a sunset, and otherwise start the search a day earlier to get it.

astronomical.description: Astronomical twilight (Sun at −18°): dusk and the following dawn, bounding the dark-sky window.

dawn_local.description: Dawn in observer-local time — the morning that ends the night — present only when a timezone was supplied.

dawn_utc.description: Dawn (Sun ascending through the depth) in ISO 8601 UTC, or null when the night never reaches the depth. It ends the night that begins at the dusk beside it: in a cycle, the morning after that cycle's set, or after its culmination when it has no set — a day later than the cycle's rise, not the dawn before it.

dusk_utc.description: Dusk (Sun descending through the depth) in ISO 8601 UTC, or null when the night never reaches the depth. It is the evening the night begins: in a cycle, the evening of that cycle's set, or after its culmination when it has no set.

night_in_progress.description: The night under way at `start`, present only when body is "sun", the Sun is below the horizon at `start`, it set since its last culmination and within the two days before, and it rises within the two days after. The first cycle then opens with the next day — at its sunrise, or its culmination when the Sun does not rise that day — and its twilight is the night after, so this field holds the night the caller is in: for each depth, dusk on the evening of that sunset and dawn before the day of the first cycle begins. Times earlier than `start` are included and have already passed. Each pair is searched only within that night, so a depth the night never reaches is null. Absent when a day the Sun never rose on fell between the last sunset and `start`: that sunset began an earlier night. A continuation call, started one second past the last set of the previous call, repeats here the night the last cycle of that call carried; its `events` do not repeat. Not one of `events` and not counted by `count`.
